summary: Learners aged 9–11 study how extreme weather events (hurricanes, tornadoes, floods, droughts, blizzards) form from specific ingredients, where each typically occurs and why, and their effects on people and landscapes. The core insight is that extreme weather is not random 'wrath' but the result of identifiable conditions — e.g. hurricanes need warm ocean water (roughly 26°C or warmer) and moisture, and weaken over land or cold sea; most strong tornadoes form from supercell thunderstorms, usually over land. A manipulable 'storm lab' where ingredients can be added or removed makes formation causal; a world map links location to ingredients; human testimony and an impact panel can serve the 'effects on people' dimension; and matching/categorising tasks assess the distinctions.
misconceptions: Hurricanes and tornadoes are basically the same — they differ hugely in scale, origin and location
Extreme weather is random punishment — each type needs specific, identifiable conditions
A hurricane can form anywhere — it needs warm ocean water (roughly ≥26°C) and won't form over cold seas or far from the tropics
Extreme weather means only storms — droughts and heatwaves are extreme events too
The 'eye' of a hurricane is the most dangerous part — it is the calm centre; the eyewall is the most violent

activities.title: Storm lab: brew a hurricane from its ingredients
steps: Set a sea-surface-temperature control, a moisture dial and an instability control (moist, unstable air), then try to 'brew' a hurricane over the ocean

Observe that in the model little happens over a cool sea; warm the water past about 26°C and add moisture, and the model storm organises, spins up and tracks across the map (real hurricanes also need other conditions, such as low wind shear and being far enough from the equator to spin)
Watch the storm begin to weaken once it moves over land or cold water, then remove one ingredient (e.g. cool the ocean) and see the storm fizzle
Explore companion mini-models: a supercell→tornado model (where strong wind shear and instability matter) and a drought model built from a rainfall deficit
Open an impact panel to see before/after effects on a community and landscape
activities.insight: Each extreme weather event needs a specific recipe of conditions; removing an ingredient stops the storm. This is exactly why hurricanes live over warm tropical seas and tornadoes cluster where air masses collide.

activities.title: Where and why: mapping events to their ingredients
steps: Use a world map showing where each event type clusters (hurricane belts over warm seas; tornado alley where air masses collide)
Match each event to the ingredients it needs and to the regions where those ingredients are common
Explain in your own words why a hurricane cannot form far from warm tropical seas
activities.insight: The location of each extreme weather event follows from where its required ingredients exist, not from chance.

activities.title: Effects on people and landscapes: in-role testimony
steps: Interview an in-role storm hunter, meteorologist, or survivor with open questions about how the storm formed, how warnings worked, and what the aftermath was
Describe at least one way the event changed the land or affected a community afterwards
Discuss how knowing the ingredients supports warning and preparedness
activities.insight: Extreme weather has serious human and environmental consequences; understanding formation conditions connects directly to warning and preparedness rather than fear.

activities.title: Check your understanding: match and categorise
steps: Match each event to its formation ingredients and to its typical location
Categorise described effects by event type
Answer the discriminator: how does a hurricane differ from a tornado in scale, lifespan, origin and location?
Decide whether the calm 'eye' of a hurricane means the danger is over
activities.insight: Hurricanes and tornadoes are related-but-different; the eye is a calm centre, not the most dangerous or final part of the storm.

checkQuestion: People sometimes use 'hurricane' and 'tornado' as if they mean the same thing. Are they the same? Pick one of them and explain how it forms and where it usually happens.
checkAnswer: They're different. A hurricane is a huge, slow storm hundreds of kilometres across that forms over warm ocean water (drawing energy from it) and can last days; a tornado is a small, violent, fast-spinning column of air that forms beneath severe thunderstorms over land and lasts minutes. Hurricanes need warm seas; tornadoes need strong thunderstorms (e.g. US 'Tornado Alley').
